# Representation and Kernel Modifications

Also called: Kernel Variants, Non-Gaussian Primitives, Negative Gaussians, Scaffold Representations

## Overview
This family modifies the fundamental geometric primitives or their mathematical kernels within the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) framework to address limitations in memory efficiency, geometric consistency, and representational expressiveness. While standard 3DGS relies on positive, isotropic/anisotropic Gaussian kernels with explicit per-primitive attribute storage, this family introduces negative color contributions for high-frequency modeling [9152-negative-gaussian-splatting], voxel-based scaffolds for memory reduction [9186-scaffold-gs], tangent-plane densification for surface smoothness [9187-geogaussian], and non-exponential Radial Basis Functions (RBFs) for broader support [9911-darbf-splatting]. These methods set themselves apart from siblings like [Base 3DGS Optimization](3761-3d-gaussian-splatting-training.md) by altering the core representation or kernel definition rather than just the training schedule or loss functions.

## Shared principles
All methods in this family operate within the differentiable rasterization pipeline of 3D Gaussian Splatting but modify one or both of the following components:
1.  **Primitive Attributes:** The data stored per Gaussian (e.g., allowing negative colors, storing attributes in a voxel grid, or predicting attributes via neural networks).
2.  **Kernel Function:** The mathematical function $K(d_M)$ used to compute the opacity/contribution of a Gaussian based on its Mahalanobis distance $d_M$ from a point in space. Standard 3DGS uses $K(d_M) = e^{-d_M^2/2}$.

The rendering equation remains the standard alpha compositing formula:
$$ C = \sum_{i \in N} c_i \alpha_i \prod_{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha_j) $$
where $N$ is the set of sorted Gaussians, $c_i$ is the color, and $\alpha_i$ is the opacity derived from the kernel evaluation. The optimization loop uses gradient descent to update the parameters of these modified primitives.

## Subtopics

### [Negative Gaussian Splatting](9152-negative-gaussian-splatting.md)
[Negative Gaussian Splatting](9152-negative-gaussian-splatting.md) extends the standard framework by allowing the color coefficient $c_i$ of any Gaussian to be negative. It operates on a joint family $G_{NeGS} = G_{GS} \cup G_{-GS}$, where $G_{GS}$ contains positive colors and $G_{-GS}$ contains negative colors. This allows two Gaussians with identical parameters and inverse colors to cancel each other out, modeling high-frequency elements and complex nonlinear structures. The method is mathematically equivalent to using "Diff-Gaussians" (differences of Gaussian distributions). The optimal coefficient $c_{opt}$ minimizing the ratio of densities $f_{m_0, \Sigma_0}$ and $f_{m_1, \Sigma_1}$ is derived via the condition $\Sigma_1^{-1}(w - m_1) = \Sigma_0^{-1}(w - m_0)$, where $w$ minimizes the quadratic function $q(x) = x^T A x + 2b^T x$ with $A = \Sigma_1^{-1} - \Sigma_0^{-1}$. It is chosen when high-frequency detail or background suppression is required.

### [Scaffold-GS](9186-scaffold-gs.md)
[Scaffold-GS](9186-scaffold-gs.md) replaces per-Gaussian attribute storage with a voxel-based scaffold representation to reduce memory usage. It initializes a 3D voxel grid from an SfM point cloud, where each voxel contains learnable features. Lightweight neural networks take interpolated voxel features as input to predict all Gaussian attributes (position, scale, rotation, opacity, color). This decouples geometric scaffolding from appearance modeling, solving the problem of redundant Gaussian proliferation in large scenes. It is chosen when memory efficiency is critical.

### [GeoGaussian](9187-geogaussian.md)
[GeoGaussian](9187-geogaussian.md) improves geometric consistency by altering the densification strategy. Instead of cloning Gaussians arbitrarily, it densifies new Gaussians on the tangent plane of existing Gaussians. It enforces local geometric continuity by adding a smoothness loss $\mathcal{L}_{smooth} = \sum_{i} \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}(i)} w_{ij} \| \mathbf{n}_i - \mathbf{n}_j \|^2$ between neighboring normals. It sets itself apart by explicitly enforcing surface smoothness during growth, unlike Negative Gaussian Splatting (which focuses on color modulation) or Scaffold-GS (which focuses on memory). It is chosen for applications requiring high-quality surface reconstruction.

### [DARBF-Splatting](9911-darbf-splatting.md)
[DARBF-Splatting](9911-darbf-splatting.md) replaces the Gaussian kernel with Decaying Anisotropic Radial Basis Functions (DARBFs), such as half-cosine or inverse multiquadric. These kernels span larger regions with higher opacity for the same variance, reducing the number of primitives needed. To preserve the computational efficiency of closed-form 2D integration, it introduces a correction factor $\psi$ (scalar or matrix) to approximate the Gaussian integration property. It is chosen when faster convergence and lower memory usage are prioritized over the specific properties of the Gaussian distribution.

### Gaussian Shell Maps
Gaussian Shell Maps (GSMs) combine CNN-based generators with 3DGS to recreate virtual humans with sophisticated details such as clothing and accessories [S1].

### Gaussian Wrapping
Gaussian Wrapping reinterprets 3D Gaussian primitives as oriented probabilistic surface elements representing geometry only within an oriented half-space, allowing derivation of closed-form occupancy, vacancy, and normal fields for watertight mesh extraction [S2].
1.  Model surface points with asymmetric primitives where the Gaussian models density decay on the outward-facing side, while the inward-facing side is considered fully occupied [S2].
2.  Identify geometric gaps where the oriented surface assumption is violated and densify the representation to obtain a watertight shell of oriented primitives [S2].
3.  Introduce a learnable oriented normal at each Gaussian element and define an adapted attenuation formulation to enable closed-form expressions for normal and occupancy fields [S2].
4.  Introduce a novel consistency loss and a dedicated densification strategy to enforce Gaussians to wrap the entire surface by closing geometric holes [S2].
5.  Modify the differentiable rasterizer to output depth as an isosurface of the continuous model [S2].
6.  Use Primal Adaptive Meshing for Region-of-Interest meshing at arbitrary resolution [S2].

## Background
3D Gaussian Splatting was introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023 as a real-time explicit scene representation [S1]. Subsequent research identified limitations in memory usage, geometric consistency, and representational flexibility. Negative Gaussian Splatting was proposed to handle high-frequency details and background suppression [S1]. Scaffold-GS was developed to address the high memory consumption of large scenes by using voxel-based scaffolds [S1]. GeoGaussian was introduced to improve surface smoothness during densification [S1]. DARBF-Splatting generalized the kernel family to include non-exponential functions for broader support [S1]. Gaussian Shell Maps and Gaussian Wrapping were developed for specific applications in human reconstruction and watertight mesh extraction, respectively [S1, S2].
